quote: Wahrscheinlich kommen so überhaupt die einfachsten Beispiele simultaner orthogonaler oder polarer Systeme zu stande.
english: Probably in this way the simplest examples of simultaneous orthogonal or polar systems arise at all.
topic: Hilbert discusses a third-order differential equation satisfied by a remainder A in simultaneous rational approximation of two functions φ, ψ, the requirement for an irrationality proof, the orthogonality property of P_n when φ, ψ are Cauchy-type integrals, and simultaneous expansion of pairs of functions in eigenfunctions with the same Fourier coefficients.

triage.modern_statement: Take two Markov/Cauchy-type functions φ(z)=∫dμ1(x)/(z−x) and ψ(z)=∫dμ2(x)/(z−x). Look for a polynomial P_n so that both P_nφ and P_nψ, minus suitable polynomials, vanish to high order at infinity. This is type II Hermite–Padé (simultaneous rational) approximation. In that setting P_n is orthogonal to lower powers of x with respect to both measures at once. Hilbert's conjecture says that this construction gives the simplest natural examples of 'simultaneous' orthogonal (or polar) systems. In modern terms these are multiple orthogonal polynomials: polynomials orthogonal with respect to several weights at the same time, as in Angelesco and Nikishin systems. This is a heuristic programmatic remark, not a sharp theorem. Hilbert's word 'polar' points to his own 1906 theory of polar integral equations, and that link is my reading; no source found here confirms it.
triage.answered_by: The idea was not answered as a stated problem. It was carried out as a theory. Hermite–Padé approximation goes back to Hermite (1873) and to Padé, Mahler and Angelesco (1919). The orthogonality view (multiple orthogonal polynomials, 'Hermite–Padé polynomials') was built up mainly by Nikishin (1980s), Aptekarev, Van Assche, Gonchar–Rakhmanov and others. Van Assche wrote surveys, including J. Comput. Appl. Math. 1999 and Contemp. Math. 236 (1999) on irrationality and transcendence. Multiple orthogonal polynomials indeed satisfy third-order differential equations, and they underlie irrationality proofs such as Apéry-type proofs and Lambert-series results. The historical names and dates in this field are from background knowledge; the search results did not confirm them.

evidence.claim: Multiple orthogonal polynomials are closely tied to Hermite–Padé approximants and are also called Hermite–Padé polynomials (survey).
Multiple orthogonal polynomials came out of Hermite–Padé approximation used in irrationality and transcendence proofs; ladder operators give differential equations for them.
Type II multiple orthogonal polynomials of hypergeometric type satisfy a third-order differential equation, which fits Hilbert's third-order ODE on the same page.
Van Assche, 'Multiple orthogonal polynomials, irrationality and transcendence', Contemp. Math. 236 (1999), applies these systems to irrationality proofs.
Survey of Padé and Hermite–Padé approximation and their orthogonality, covering Angelesco and Nikishin systems.
Strong asymptotics of multiple orthogonal polynomials for Angelesco systems is still being studied (2024).

triage.why: The page links simultaneous rational approximation of two Cauchy-type integrals, orthogonality of P_n, a third-order ODE and irrationality proofs. Together these match what is now called multiple orthogonal polynomials / Hermite–Padé approximation (Angelesco and Nikishin systems). That theory became the standard source of 'simultaneous orthogonal systems', so in substance Hilbert's expectation came true. It is not one of Hilbert's published problems. Hilbert's remark is vague, so there is no precise theorem that 'answers' it. No source cites this diary entry, and the meaning of 'polar systems' and the exact link to Hilbert are uncertain. The confidence is medium for these reasons.
